response.text:
Recent work supports separating observable behavior from user intent. [Beyond Explicit and Implicit (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09869) distinguishes intentional feedback from ordinary interaction traces; [Rethinking the Evaluation of Dialogue Systems (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12994) examines how follow-up user feedback changes judgments of relevance and usefulness. Implication: history similarity supports broad relatedness, but cannot establish a reason to choose an item now. Compatibility, redundancy, mood and current demand should remain unknown without explicit supporting evidence.

A proposed annotation scheme for the twenty users: record candidate identity confidence, history-supported relatedness, explicit acceptance/rejection, stated current need, rejection reason, missing evidence and confidence, with an evidence excerpt for each judgment. Keep ambiguous identity, insufficient information and explicit rejection separate. Validate using users’ own independent judgments of relatedness and “would choose now,” followed by neutral pairwise comparisons with ties and abstention. Randomize presentation, adjudicate annotation disagreements, and report agreement and proxy precision separately by category. These are design recommendations informed by [ConSiDERS-The-Human (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.63/), which emphasizes clear scoring criteria, cognitive uncertainty and evaluation bias.

Hard negatives require particular caution: [Enhanced Bayesian Personalized Ranking (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) identifies false negatives as a source of misleading training signals. A related but unchosen item is therefore a comparison candidate, not a confirmed rejection. Validate diagnostic proxies against human feedback before using them as supervision; [Soboroff (2025)](https://www.nist.gov/publications/dont-use-llms-make-relevance-judgments) cautions against replacing human relevance judgments with LLM-generated labels.
